explanation: The Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome (also known as the Marcus Gunn phenomenon) is a trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis. Strabismus and amblyopia are common associations, occurring in about half of patients. The strabismus may be comitant, but noncomitant forms are also frequently encountered, including double-elevator palsy and superior rectus palsy. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, but with incomplete penetrance. The movement that most commonly causes elevation of the ptotic eyelid is lateral mandibular movement to the contralateral side. This phenomenon is usually ﬁrst noticed by the mother when she is feeding the baby.

question: What ﬁnding is an indication for urgent surgical intervention in a pediatric orbital ﬂoor fracture?

explanation: Upon fracture of the orbital ﬂoor, orbital contents may prolapse into the maxillary sinus and become entrapped. Restriction occurs with entrapment of the inferior rectus beneath either a trapdoor fracture or a linear opening caused by ﬂexion deformity of the ﬂoor. Injury to the inferior rectus muscle or to its nerve, with resulting weakness, may be caused by hemorrhage or ischemia, in addition to restriction. If muscle entrapment is present, a forced duction test shows restriction of passive movement of the eye. Eye movement may stimulate the oculocardiac reﬂex, causing pain, nausea, and bradycardia. question: What surgical procedure may result in continued orbital expansion in a child born with a microphthalmic eye?
explanation: Dermis-fat grafting, when placed at an early age, may continue to grow with the child, resulting in progressive orbital expansion and minimizing hypoplasia of the orbit. A large implant, with or without enucleation, may improve the hypoplastic orbit in the short term, and maintain the volume, but it will not expand over time. An enophthalmic wedge may be used in an adult to correct enophthalmos from microphthalmos, but is not recommended in a child.

question: A 59-year-old man presents with a painful, enlarging mass on his right lower eyelid for the past 4 months. Squamous cell carcinoma is known to metastasize through direct extension through nerves. In this case, the tumor spread along the infraorbital nerve to the cavernous sinus. This also explains why the patient has pain. Squamous cell carcinoma is less common than basal cell carcinoma, but it is more aggressive. The tumor may arise spontaneously or from actinic keratosis. Immunodeﬁcient patients are at increased risk. Treatment without evidence of metastasis is surgical excision with wide margins sent for pathology. In cases with suspected metastasis, orbital exenteration and oncology consultation may be warranted. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common eyelid malignancy. Risk factors include light skin, smoking, and prolonged history of sun exposure. Management is incisional or excisional biopsy. Although metastasis is rare, basal cell tumors can invade the orbit if treated inadequately. What is the most common bacterial pathogen in acute dacryocystitis?
explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of acute dacryocystitis. Other gram-positive bacteria, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, occur less commonly. Gram- negative organisms may cause disease in patients who are diabetic or immunocompromised, or in nursing home environments with atypical pathogens present. Actinomyces israelii is the most common cause of acute canaliculitis. The most common cause of acute dacryocystitis is a complete nasolacrimal duct obstruction that leads to tear stasis and infection. Complications of dacryocystitis include dacryocystocele, chronic conjunctivitis, and cellulitis. Probing and irrigation of the nasolacrimal duct should be avoided until the infection resolves, as it can be extremely painful. Empiric treatment is with oral antibiotics, most commonly with amoxicillin (Augmentin) or cephalexin (Keﬂex). Any abscess formation should be incised and drained and left open to heal by second intention. If the infection does not clear with oral antibiotics, a dacryocystorhinostomy is often required to relieve the obstruction.

question: A 45-year-old male complains of pain around the right orbit that began 9 months ago. His computed tomography (CT) scan is shown in Figure 1. What is the best next step in management of this patient's condition?

explanation: The CT scan shows a lacrimal gland mass with calciﬁcation and adjacent bony thinning/erosion (The lacrimal gland fossa on the right is larger and more “scalloped” compared to contralateral fossa.). These ﬁndings, coupled with the history of pain, are highly suspicious for a primary lacrimal gland malignancy, most likely adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC). Dacryoadenitis, a form of idiopathic orbital inﬂammatory syndrome (IOIS), does not typically present with chronic pain and does not cause bone erosion. Orbital lymphoma is also unlikely for the same reasons, although it should be noted that inﬂammatory signs or pain can be present in up to 25% of orbital lymphomas, and aggressive subtypes can show bony erosion on CT. Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) may cause expansion of the lacrimal gland fossa (“fossa formation”), but not frank erosion, and is usually an indolent, painless process. The key issue here is whether or not to excise the lesion completely or to simply perform an incisional biopsy for diagnosis. If pleomorphic adenoma is suspected, the ENTIRE lesion must be excised. Incompletely excised pleomorphic adenomas have a higher recurrence rate, will be more diﬃcult to excise if they recur, and can undergo malignant transformation. Complete excision of an ACC can require exenteration and radical orbitectomy with removal of the roof, lateral wall, and ﬂoor along with the overlying soft tissues. There is no evidence that this disﬁguring approach or other aggressive treatment such as radiation, chemotherapy, or a combination of these modalities improves prognosis. question: What anatomic relationship of the periorbita contributes to the formation of a subperiosteal abscess?

explanation: The periorbita is simply another name for the periosteum of the orbit. As periosteum travels toward the orbit along the facial bones, it fuses at the orbital rim to form the arcus marginalis, which is ﬁrmly tethered to the underlying bone and serves as the take-oﬀ point for the orbital septum (which may be considered an extension of the periosteum). The periorbita extends posteriorly into the orbit from the arcus marginalis as an avascular layer that is loosely attached to underlying bone except at the major orbital ostia (superior and inferior orbital ﬁssures, optic canal). The loose attachment allows for a potential subperiosteal space for pus or blood (subperiosteal abscess or hematoma). The periorbita is relatively impermeable, sequestering blood or pus. Posteriorly, periorbita fuses with the dura of the optic nerve at the optic canal.

explanation: Orbital ﬂoor fractures (blowout fractures) are rarely an emergent or urgent pathology. Large fractures that cause signiﬁcant globe dystopia (enophthalmos and/or hypoglobus) can be repaired successfully 1-3 weeks after injury. The one major exception is the so-called "white-eyed blowout fracture" that occurs primarily in children. Because the pediatric orbital skeleton has not fully calciﬁed, the bones are pliable and can "greenstick" (wherein one side of a bone is broken and the other is bent), rather than break cleanly. This results in a trapdoor eﬀect along the orbital ﬂoor or, less commonly, the medial wall: A narrow fracture opens, allowing fat and/or rectus muscle to herniate into the maxillary/ethmoid sinus, and then the trapdoor fracture snaps shut, tightly entrapping soft tissue and potentially causing signiﬁcant muscle ischemia. The fracture is termed "white-eyed" because the patient has few if any of the usual signs of orbital trauma: There is almost no ecchymosis or eyelid edema. The tightly entrapped muscle typically causes a severe vasovagal reaction from the oculocardiac reﬂex when the child tries to move his/her eyes, resulting in nausea, vomiting, poor oral intake, and bradycardia. There is no known eﬀective treatment for the classic indirect traumatic optic neuropathy (TON) seen in a deceleration injury. explanation: Cicatricial entropion can be caused by conditions such as cicatricial pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, trachoma, herpes zoster virus, enucleation, posterior-approach ptosis correction, thermal or chemical burns, and other scarring conditions. The vertical tarsoconjunctival contracture and internal rotation of the eyelid margins causes irritation to the globe and requires correction. The goal of treatment is to eliminate the chronic ocular irritation by removing the lashes and keratinized tissue from contact with the globe and cornea. Minor inversion of the eyelid can be corrected by resection of anterior lamellar tissue with or without mucous membrane grafting. More extensive forniceal shortening and distortion of eyelid structures requires grafting to reconstruct the conjunctiva. Most commonly used and successful grafts are either a buccal mucous membrane graft or an amniotic membrane graft. In this case, the patient is not a candidate for buccal mucous membrane grafting, so the preferred graft would be amniotic membrane. Skin grafts would not be used for conjunctival reconstruction, but rather for anterior lamellar reconstruction.

explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from pleuripotent mesenchymal cells, not from extraocular muscles. The average age of onset is 5-7 years, and patients typically present with rapidly progressive, unilateral painless proptosis. There are 4 diﬀerent variants of rhabdomyosarcoma. Alveolar accounts for only 9% of orbital rhabdomyosarcomas and is the most malignant form. It has a tendency to develop in the inferior orbit. Embryonal is the most common type and accounts for more than 80% of cases. It has a predilection for a superonasal location in the orbit and has a very high survival rate (94%). Pleomorphic is the rarest form. It is also the most well- diﬀerentiated form and consequently has the highest survival rate (97%). The botryoid variant of rhabdomyosarcoma is quite rare. It is unique in that it does not occur as a primary orbital tumor, but rather invades the orbit from the adjacent paranasal sinuses or from the conjunctiva. Treatment of rhabdomyosarcoma requires surgical debulking, chemotherapy, and radiation. Intravenous corticosteroids should be infused for 24 hours to decrease orbital inﬂammation; ice packs should be used to reduce swelling.

question: A 6-year-old child has had painless proptosis for 2 weeks and has undergone a computed tomography (CT) scan, which is shown in the ﬁgure. What diagnosis is most likely?

explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) should always be high on the diﬀerential diagnosis list of painless proptosis occurring in a child. The average age of orbital RMS presentation is 5 to 7 years, but RMS may also occur in younger or older children. Recognition of the possibility of orbital RMS is important because urgent biopsy for histopathologic conﬁrmation is important in successful management; spread of tumor into the paranasal sinuses or cranial vault worsens prognosis. Of note, a minority of orbital RMS cases may present with pain and other inﬂammatory signs that may be diﬃcult to diﬀerentiate from idiopathic orbital inﬂammatory syndrome (IOIS). The most common cause of unilateral proptosis in a child is orbital cellulitis. However, orbital cellulitis typically presents clinically with pain and erythema, and radiographically with signiﬁcant sinus opaciﬁcation. Neither is seen in the photographs. Similarly, IOIS presents with sudden onset of pain. A retained orbital foreign body should also present with symptoms of pain and erythema, either from sterile or infectious inﬂammation. Of note, a retained orbital foreign body should always be considered in the diﬀerential diagnosis of a pediatric orbital mass, even without a clear history of trauma.

question: A 75-year-old patient has lower lid laxity, a preseptal orbicularis muscle that overrides the pretarsal orbicularis muscle, and disinserted lower lid retractors. This constellation of clinical features predisposes the patient to what condition?

An 85-year-old diabetic inpatient reports new-onset right-sided orbital pain and blurred vision. An ear-nose- throat (otolaryngologist) colleague has noted a necrotic eschar in the nasal cavity with overlying focal tissue necrosis. The patient was initially admitted for cancer chemotherapy. What would be the most likely diagnosis? Horizontal lower eyelid laxity destabilizes the eyelid margin and predisposes the patient to involutional ectropion or entropion. Once the lower eyelid retractors become disinserted, vertical laxity occurs, typically manifesting as entropion. A vicious cycle begins as the lashes rub and irritate the cornea, which then causes inner contracture and spasm of the orbicularis oculi muscle as a protective mechanism. Because of the vertical instability, the preseptal orbicularis overrides the pretarsal orbicularis, causing even more inturning of the lid margin and lashes. Orbicularis override is also referred to as spastic entropion. Cicatricial entropion and ectropion are deﬁned by shortening of either the anterior or posterior lamella. The anterior lamella consists of skin and orbicularis oculi muscle and any cicatrix in this layer (skin scarring from trauma, burns, surgery, etc.) will result in out-turning of the eyelid (ectropion). The posterior lamella is composed of tarsus and conjunctiva, and shortening (ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, etc.) will result in cicatricial entropion.

explanation: In patients with metabolic acidosis, diabetes mellitus, or malignancies, or patients who are undergoing treatment with antimetabolites or steroids, it is necessary to consider zygomycosis (also known as phycomycosis or mucormycosis) fungal disease. These fungi extend into the orbit from an adjacent sinus or the nasal cavity. Orbital involvement can present with proptosis and orbital apex syndrome (internal and external ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, decreased corneal sensation, and decreased vision). They invade blood vessel walls, leading to a thrombosing vasculitis. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed by biopsy of the necrotic-appearing tissues in the nasopharynx or involved sinus or orbit. On histology, zygomycosis shows nonseptate large branching hyphae.

question: A patient with stable thyroid disease has new horizontal and vertical diplopia, which worsens at the end of the day. Lid retraction is less obvious than in the past. What would best explain these ﬁndings?
explanation: A variable strabismus that worsens later in the day or with fatigue and is associated with ptosis is indicative of myasthenia gravis, in which acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause muscle weakness and strabismus. It can occur in patients with thyroid eye disease. Worsening thyroid eye disease can cause a worsening strabismus, but it should be stable throughout the day and associated with worsening lid retraction. Third nerve palsy can cause ptosis and new-onset diplopia, but it would be stable over the day. A decompensated phoria should not aﬀect the lid position.

question: What is the most common pathogen associated with canaliculitis?
explanation: Infection within the canaliculus is caused by a variety of bacteria, viruses, and mycotic organisms. The most common pathogen is a ﬁlamentous gram-positive rod, Actinomyces israelii. The other pathogens listed (Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) can cause canaliculitis, but are not the most common causes.

question: A 45-year-old woman who experienced blunt trauma to her right orbit 1 week ago presents with a droopy right lid. On examination, she has an MRD-1 of 1.5 mm and levator function of 5 mm. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU and there are no pupillary abnormalities. There is no evidence of orbital hemorrhage, exophthalmos, or ophthalmoplegia. The remainder of her ocular examination is normal. What is the best assessment of her injury and approach to treatment? &

options.A: She has traumatic ptosis, and observation for at least 6 months should be allowed to assess for spontaneous recovery before surgical intervention.
options.B: She has paralytic ptosis due to a levator injury and should have frontalis sling surgery if there is no spontaneous improvement in the next 2 months.
options.C: She has paralytic lagophthalmos due to a facial nerve injury. She should allow for 3 months of observation to assess for spontaneous recovery before surgical intervention.
options.D: She has an injury to the facial nerve resulting in traumatic ptosis. She should undergo frontalis sling ptosis repair if there is no improvement within 6 months.

explanation: The clinical scenario describes a traumatic ptosis from blunt trauma. Traumatic ptosis can result from a number of etiologies, including damage to the oculomotor nerve, carotid dissection with a secondary Horner syndrome, blunt or lacerating injury to the levator muscle, or eyelid edema. Injury to the facial nerve would cause brow ptosis or lagophthalmos due to orbicularis oculi weakness. However, the levator muscle would remain intact, allowing the patient to open her eyelid. Traumatic ptosis from blunt injury should be followed conservatively for at least 6 months. The majority of patients will experience either partial or complete spontaneous recovery of eyelid function. If the levator muscle does not recover after that time, surgical intervention can be considered.

question: Why are orbital roof fractures more likely to occur in young children than in adults?

options.A: There is over-projection of the midface in young children.
options.B: The frontal lobe is underdeveloped in young children.
options.C: There is a larger cranial vault-to- midface ratio in young children.
options.D: There is better pneumatization of frontal sinuses in young children.

explanation: Orbital roof fractures occur much more commonly in young children than adults for 2 main reasons. First, pneumatized frontal sinuses, the structures that absorb much of the force of a frontal blow in adults, are not yet developed in children. This absence of pneumatized frontal sinuses allows force to be transferred directly to the orbital roof, resulting in fracture. Second, an infant or toddler has a much higher cranial vault-to- face ratio than an adult (8:1 vs 2:1, respectively) along with a ﬂatter face, lacking the midfacial and nasal projection of adults. This results in a larger and more prominent forehead that is more susceptible to injury. The frontal lobe is not underdeveloped in young children.

question: A toddler presents with ptosis and a chin-up position. What is the most important determinant in choosing the surgical technique for repair?
explanation: The levator function is the most important determinant of the type of surgical repair to employ. Moderate to good levator function can often beneﬁt from a levator resection. Poor levator function requires a frontalis sling approach to recruit the brow musculature to lift the lid.

In this patient, the diplopia is worse in downgaze because of restriction of the thickened superior rectus muscle. About 5% to 10% of patients with thyroid eye disease may develop optic neuropathy, most commonly from crowding at the orbital apex. Upper-eyelid retraction is common in thyroid eye disease and ptosis is rare (unless coexistent myasthenia gravis is present). question: What is the primary treatment regimen for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma?

With radiation and chemotherapy, survival rates are better than 90% if the orbital tumor has not invaded or extended beyond the bony orbital walls. They are more prevalent in children whose frontal sinuses have not yet pneumatized (the mature frontal sinuses serve as an impact crumple zone in adults). Early diplopia is usually from a hematoma or orbital swelling. Muscle entrapment is very rare with orbital roof fractures. Optic neuropathy is uncommon. The microscopic description diﬀerentiates pleomorphic adenoma, an epithelial tumor, from benign lymphoproliferative disease, which may have a similar course, but it is not an epithelial tumor. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a highly malignant tumor that microscopically may have benign-appearing cells of basaloid or cribriform morphology that are growing in tubules, solid nests, or Swiss-cheese pattern. question: A 32-year-old woman has a chronic unilateral conjunctivitis unresponsive to intermittent topical steroid and sulfonamide treatment. Examination reveals a follicular conjunctivitis and a 2 mm ﬂesh-colored dome- shaped mass on the eyelid margin with a small central crater. What is the provisional diagnosis?
explanation: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of the epithelium resulting in dome-shaped, waxy epidermal nodules with a central umbilication. On histopathology, these lesions are very distinctive, with nodular thickening of the epithelium and necrotic cells at the center of the nodule being extruded at the skin surface. As the replicating virus ﬁlls the cytoplasm, a large viral inclusion (molluscum body) forms and displaces the nucleus to the cell periphery. These bodies are eosinophilic at the base of the lesion and become more basophilic as they migrate to the surface. The virus-ﬁlled cells shed into the fornix cause a follicular reaction of the conjunctiva. Eyelid lesions and a follicular conjunctivitis may be present in herpetic blepharoconjunctivitis, but herpetic lesions are vesicular rather than ﬂeshy and umbilicated. Basal cell carcinoma and amelanotic melanoma may also present with lesions of the eyelid margin, but these lesions do not typically have an associated conjunctivitis.

question: A 60-year-old man has severe canalicular stenosis. Appropriate management would include what option?

In CDCR, a ﬁstula is created between the conjunctiva in the area of the caruncle through the lacrimal sac and its bony fossa into the nasal cavity. A Pyrex Jones tube is inserted into this tract to maintain patency. For mild canalicular stenosis, probing and dilation, sometimes with silicone intubation, can be attempted. A successful DCR requires patent canaliculi. A 3-snip punctoplasty is an excellent treatment option for punctal stenosis, but would fail in the face of more distal canalicular stenosis. Topical corticosteroids would also prove unsuccessful.

question: In a patient with acquired epiphora, what would a soft stop indicate during careful probing of the lower canaliculus, where the examiner uses lateral traction to straighten the canaliculus? widening of the horizontal palpebral ﬁssure B. 17 Your Answer rounding of the lateral canthus C.
explanation: The presence of a "soft stop" when probing the canaliculus can represent a kink in the tissue, caused by bunching of the soft tissues in front of the probe tip. However, if careful probing, including lateral traction to straighten the canaliculus, still reveals a soft stop, then the diagnosis is complete obstruction of the canaliculus. With patency of the canalicular system, the examiner would detect a "hard stop," indicating that the probe reached the medial wall of the lacrimal fossa. With obstruction of the nasolacrimal sac, the examiner would detect a hard stop; however, irrigation would reveal reﬂux through the canalicular system. With patency of the nasolacrimal sac, the examiner would detect a hard stop, and irrigation would not show signiﬁcant reﬂux, as most of the irrigation ﬂuid would pass freely into the nasopharynx.

question: Examination of a 70-year-old patient discloses loss of eyelashes in conjunction with a thickened eyelid. Appropriate management consists of what procedure?
explanation: This clinical scenario typiﬁes the ominous "masquerade syndrome" of sebaceous carcinoma (also termed sebaceous gland carcinoma, sebaceous cell carcinoma, sebaceous adenocarcinoma, meibomian gland carcinoma) arises from sebaceous glands. The 2 sebaceous glands present in the periocular region are the meibomian glands of the tarsal plate and the glands of Zeis that lie along the cilia of the lid; both are examples of holocrine glands. question: A patient arrives in the trauma bay after a motor vehicle crash in which he hit his face on the dashboard. He has ecchymosis and signiﬁcant swelling to his right eye. The eyelids are rock hard to the touch. He complains of blurry vision in the right eye. His visual acuity is 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS. He can see 6/11 color plates OD and 11/11 OS. What is the most appropriate next step? adenocarcinoma, meibomian gland carcinoma), which is a highly malignant and potentially lethal tumor that arises from the meibomian glands of the tarsal plate, the glands of Zeis associated with the eyelashes, or the sebaceous glands of the facial skin, eyebrow, or caruncle. Early in the course of the disease, patients can present with nonspeciﬁc ﬁndings of blepharitis, madarosis, and eyelid thickening. Since sebaceous carcinoma can arise from the tarsal plate or the eyelid margin, superﬁcial shave biopsies may miss the underlying tumor, and a full-thickness biopsy is recommended for diagnosis. The treatment of sebaceous carcinoma is wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery. Because skip areas and pagetoid spread are common in sebaceous carcinoma, map biopsies of the conjunctiva may be considered. If pagetoid spread is present, then adjuvant cryotherapy may be used. External beam radiotherapy is not recommended for treatment of sebaceous carcinoma, as these tumors are relatively radioresistant.

explanation: To preserve visual function, immediate canthotomy and cantholysis should be performed to release the retrobulbar hemorrhage. The compartment syndrome eﬀect caused by hemorrhage in the orbit leads to optic nerve compression and compromised arterial perfusion. This patient is experiencing increased intraocular pressure as well as decreased visual acuity and color vision, which suggests optic nerve involvement. The most appropriate next step is to intervene with a canthotomy and cantholysis. The other options would only delay deﬁnitive treatment.

question: A 60-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes presents with progressively worsening double vision and severe periorbital pain that began 2 days ago. One day prior, she noted that the double vision resolved. Severe vision loss to no light perception is noted on the left, along with a fundus examination consistent with an ophthalmic artery occlusion. Computed tomography (CT) of orbits shows extensive opaciﬁcation of the left maxillary sinus extending into the orbital apex. What would a biopsy most likely show?
explanation: Few orbital and paranasal sinus processes progress to rapid and profound visual loss. Chief among these is zygomycosis (mucormycosis), a fungus with a propensity to invade blood vessel walls, producing thrombosing vasculitis. Tissue necrosis then promotes further fungal invasion. Predisposing factors include systemic disease or treatments associated with metabolic acidosis and immunosuppression (diabetes, malignancy, chemotherapy, and corticosteroids). Tissue is usually obtained to conﬁrm the diagnosis. Histology shows nonseptate, large branching hyphae that stain with hematoxylin-eosin. Presenting signs often include proptosis and orbital apex syndrome (internal/external ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, decreased corneal sensation, and profound and rapidly progressive visual loss. Pain is also a hallmark of the disease, presumably due to soft tissue ischemia (“orbital angina”). Treatment is aimed at control of underlying metabolic or immunologic abnormality and local surgical debridement. Antifungal therapy is given via intravenous administration of amphotericin B or liposomal amphotericin B. Bacterial infection rarely presents with this tempo of clinical progression, with one major exception being odontogenic orbital cellulitis (orbital infection from an infected tooth), which can rapidly spread into the orbit and skull base via the paranasal sinuses and venous plexuses. Necrotizing fasciitis, an extremely aggressive infection from the skin, typically involves more superﬁcial layers of the lids and perhaps anterior orbit, but infrequently spreads to the orbital apex early in the disease course. Orbital lymphoproliferative disease has a fairly indolent presentation in the vast majority of cases. On occasion, an aggressive primary or secondary (from an adjacent paranasal sinus) diﬀuse large B-cell or mantle cell lymphoma can present with sudden visual loss, but histopathology would not show a pleomorphic inﬁltrate. Similarly, metastatic disease to the orbital apex would only rarely present with rapidly progressive visual loss and would typically not present with concomitant maxillary sinus involvement. In the case presented, the primary concern for the clinician must be mucormycosis, and it requires urgent work-up and management.

question: The patient shown in the photo presents with a history of dry eye and chalazion incision and drainage. He wants the ophthalmologist to excise the rotten annoyance again. He admits that he is not consistent with warm compresses and lid scrubs. What would be the most appropriate procedure or treatment recommendation at this time?
explanation: Carcinoma of the sebaceous glands is highly malignant. It can be missed, since it may simulate the more common chalazia and chronic blepharitis. (It can also be confused with basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma, mucous membrane pemphigoid, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, or pannus associated with adult inclusion conjunctivitis.) Sebaceous adenocarcinoma can arise from meibomian glands in the tarsal plate, glands of Zeis (associated with eyelashes) (see Figure 1 for eyelid anatomy review) or sebaceous glands of the caruncle, eyebrow or facial skin. In the photograph, there is a yellow lesion in the upper eyelid on the margin and tarsal conjunctiva. It is yellow due to lipid material, which may prompt the examiner to think of sebaceous gland carcinoma (the neoplastic cells have lipid material within them); however, the sign, along with the history of the recurrent chalazion, that must lead the examiner to suspect malignancy is the associated loss of eyelashes (madarosis) in the area of the lesion. The tumor typically destroys the follicles of the cilia and thus eyelashes can no longer be supported. Eﬀacement of the meibomian gland oriﬁces also occurs, as can be seen in the photograph. (Of note, per the BCSC, staphylococcal blepharitis can also cause madarosis; thus, it is worth pointing out that having the history of a nodule that then causes madarosis is more characteristic of sebaceous adenocarcinoma.) It is also good to be aware that marked conjunctival inﬂammation and hyperemia may be present with sebaceous carcinoma, especially with pagetoid spread of tumor cells. Pagetoid spread may be seen on examination as a ﬁne papillary elevation of the tarsal conjunctiva. Intraepidermal growth may lead to extension from the tarsal plate across the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva and even onto cornea with replacement of corneal epithelium with tumor cells. To evaluate for sebaceous adenocarcinoma, a full-thickness eyelid biopsy or full-thickness tarsal punch biopsy is recommended, as the lesion may originate in the tarsal plate or in the eyelid margin. question: A 15-year-old boy presents with 2 pearly ulcerated lesions with rolled edges on his face. The patient also has lesions on the palms of his hands. explanation: Basal cell nevus syndrome, also known as Gorlin syndrome, aﬀects 0.7% of patients with basal cell carcinoma. This autosomal dominant syndrome results in multiple nevoid BCC in young patients aged 10 to 30 years old. The syndrome also causes odontogenic jaw cysts, skeletal abnormalities, palmar and plantar pits, neurologic abnormalities, and endocrine disorders. Sudden onset of multiple seborrheic keratoses is known as the Leser-Trélat sign and is associated with systemic malignancy, usually a gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.

question: What ﬁnding on orbital imaging is suggestive of a carotid- cavernous ﬁstula?
explanation: Carotid-cavernous ﬁstula (CCF) is an abnormal communication between the venous plexus of the cavernous sinus and the internal carotid artery (ICA), the external carotid artery (ECA), or both. A variety of classiﬁcation schema exist, but for the ophthalmologist a designation of direct (ICA directly feeding the cavernous sinus) or indirect (a branch of the ICA/ECA feeding the cavernous sinus) CCF suﬃces. The major venous drainage for the orbit is via the superior ophthalmic vein (SOV) into the cavernous sinus. If the cavernous sinus is backed up with arterial blood, orbital outﬂow is blocked, with resultant congestive orbitopathy, arterialization of the conjunctival vessels, and increased intraocular pressure from increased episcleral venous pressure. Typical ﬁndings of CCF on computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are enlargement of the SOV and mild to moderate enlargement of the extraocular muscles from venous engorgement (sometimes confused with thyroid eye disease). The angular vein may be enlarged on cerebral arteriography, but typically does not manifest on CT or MRI. Neither the optic nerve sheath nor the ophthalmic artery shows abnormality on imaging. On occasion, MRI may also show thrombus within the SOV if spontaneous closure is occurring.

question: A full-thickness upper eyelid blepharotomy is created 13.5 mm above the eyelid margin in a 45-year-old woman with no surgical history and an upper eyelid crease of 9 mm above the eyelid margin. Through what structures does this incision pass, from anterior to posterior?

options.A: skin, orbicularis oculi, retro- orbicularis oculi fat, orbital septum, levator muscle, Müller muscle, conjunctiva
options.B: skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, capsulopalpebral fascia, Müller muscle, conjunctiva
options.C: skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, orbital fat, levator aponeurosis, Müller muscle, conjunctiva
options.D: skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, orbital fat, levator aponeurosis, Müller muscle, tarsus, conjunctiva

explanation: "Skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, capsulopalpebral fascia, Müller muscle, conjunctiva" is incorrect because the capsulopalpebral fascia is a lower eyelid structure and the levator aponeurosis is left out here. "Skin, orbicularis oculi, retro- orbicularis oculi fat, orbital septum, levator muscle, Müller muscle, conjunctiva" is incorrect because retro-orbicularis oculi fat is superior to the incision, and the levator muscle has already become the levator aponeurosis at the level of the incision. "Skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, orbital fat, levator aponeurosis, Müller muscle, tarsus, conjunctiva" is incorrect because the lid incision is superior to the tarsus. The skin on the eyelids is the thinnest skin in the body, lacking subcutaneous tissue. Posterior to the skin lies the orbicularis oculi muscle, divided into pretarsal, preseptal, and orbital portions. The pretarsal portion sits anterior to the tarsus, as the name would suggest, from the lid margin superiorly about 10 mm, to the superior edge of the tarsus near the lid crease. Superior to the upper lid crease, the orbicularis lies anterior to the orbital septum, an extension of periosteum from the arcus marginalis at the orbital rim. Posterior to the orbital septum lie 2 orbital fat pads in the upper eyelid and the lacrimal gland laterally. The fat pads are just anterior to the levator muscle and aponeurosis. In white patients, the orbital septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis superior to the superior tarsal border. This marks the ﬁrst time the anterior levator ﬁbers are not bordered anteriorly by orbital fat and septum; as a result, their anterior extensions through the pretarsal orbicularis form the lid crease, which is 7-10 mm superior to the margin in the non-Asian eyelid. Müller muscle, the other upper eyelid retractor, originates from the posterior surface of the levator muscle 14 mm superior to the superior tarsal border, approximating Whitnall ligament. This muscle inserts on the superior tarsus. Posterior to Müller muscle lies the conjunctiva, which extends inferiorly on the posterior side of the tarsus to the lid margin. In Asian eyelids, the septum fuses with the pretarsal levator aponeurosis and the orbital fat approaches the eyelid margin as a result, explaining the location of the Asian lid crease several millimeters from the eyelid margin.

question: A 50-year-old patient has a mass in the left upper eyelid. Examination shows an enlarged, nontender lacrimal gland without periorbital edema. What echographic characteristic would support a diagnosis of lymphoma rather than pleomorphic adenoma?
explanation: Low internal reﬂectivity indicates that the lesion is homogeneous, consistent with the histology of lymphoma. Other ultrasound features of orbital lymphoma include variable shape, regular internal structure, weak attenuation, and ﬁrm consistency. In contrast, pleomorphic adenoma of the lacrimal gland orbital lobe demonstrates medium-to-high internal reﬂectivity on orbital ultrasound. Other features are ovoid or round shape, high pulsatility, moderate sound attenuation, and ﬁrm consistency. Pleomorphic adenomas may contain cysts.

question: A 64-year-old woman presents following an episode of transient vision loss in her right eye. Associated clinical history includes recent headaches, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. Her vision and intraocular pressure are normal, and the clinical examination shows mild refractive error, but the anterior segment and fundoscopic examination results are otherwise normal. What clinical laboratory test is considered to be most speciﬁc in conﬁrming the etiology?
explanation: This patient's clinical symptoms are highly suspicious for giant cell arteritis (GCA) or temporal arteritis. When evaluating patients whose clinical symptoms are suspicious for GCA, diagnostic testing should begin with laboratory tests of ESR, CRP, and CBC. CRP is a sensitive indicator of inﬂammation and is typically obtained in conjunction with the ESR; however, the ESR may be normal in up to 16% of cases of GCA. CRP may increase diagnostic accuracy of GCA because it may be more speciﬁc and less aﬀected by increasing age and anemia when compared to ESR. CBC is obtained in order to evaluate for thrombocytosis (increased platelet count), which may suggest active disease, but is not speciﬁc to GCA. Fasting blood glucose testing is useful to determine the etiology of clinical ﬁndings suggestive of diabetic retinopathy changes but has limited value in temporal arteritis.

explanation: Arteriovenous ﬁstulas are acquired lesions caused by abnormal direct communication between an artery and a vein. This may be secondary to trauma or degeneration. The 2 forms are carotid cavernous ﬁstula and dural cavernous ﬁstula. The carotid cavernous ﬁstula is typically associated with trauma such as basal skull fracture, whereas the dural ﬁstula occurs more often in older patients with systemic hypertension and atherosclerosis. Proptosis and compressive optic neuropathy can occur in both and are considered an indication for urgent intervention. Exophthalmos, arterialization of episcleral venules, elevated cavernous sinus pressure with III, IV, or VI nerve palsy, and elevated intraocular pressure may occur, but they do not require urgent intervention.

question: The medial orbital wall includes what orbital bones?

options.A: greater wing of sphenoid and zygomatic
options.B: frontal and lesser wing of sphenoid

explanation: The medial orbital wall is composed of 4 bones: the sphenoid (lesser wing), maxillary, ethmoid, and the lacrimal (mnemonic: SMEL, since the medial wall is close to the nose). The frontal bone and lesser wing of the sphenoid make up the orbital roof (mnemonic: "front-less").

question: What is the term for adhesions between conjunctival surfaces due to inﬂammation, trauma, or previous surgery?
explanation: Symblepharon refers to adhesion of conjunctival surfaces. Entropion refers to an inward turning of the lid margin. Euryblepharon refers to vertical shortening and horizontal lengthening of the aﬀected eyelid. Trachoma is one of several causes of symblepharon.

question: What prophylactic treatment is frequently used to prevent scarring after laser skin resurfacing?
explanation: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) outbreaks may occur after laser skin resurfacing, which could lead to signiﬁcant scarring. Most physicians prophylactically treat patients with perioperative oral antiviral agents. Oral, not topical, antivirals are necessary to suppress outbreaks of HSV. Selection of appropriate patients for laser skin resurfacing is imperative. Isotretinoin inhibits reepithelialization, and is therefore contraindicated in laser resurfacing if used within 12 months prior to laser treatment.

question: What technique is used to evaluate the stability of the tear ﬁlm?
explanation: Tear breakup time is a way of assessing the stability of the tear ﬁlm. This can be observed after ﬂuorescein has been placed in the conjunctival cul-de-sac. The patient is asked to open his or her eyes and refrain from blinking. The ophthalmologist then examines the tear ﬁlm using a broad beam of the slit lamp. The time before breakup should be at least 10 seconds. An enlarged tear ﬁlm meniscus may suggest deﬁciency of lacrimal outﬂow, and observation of the lacrimal lake may demonstrate precipitated proteins or debris that may indicate an abnormal tear ﬁlm. The basal tear secretion test is used to measure tear secretion. The dye disappearance test is useful for assessing the presence or absence of adequate lacrimal outﬂow.

question: In a 3-month-old child, what is an advantage of in-oﬃce probing and irrigation of the nasolacrimal duct?
explanation: Nasolacrimal duct probing is a common surgical procedure. Some ophthalmologists recommend early probing of the infant in the oﬃce. Advantages of early probing include avoidance of general anesthesia and hospitalization, as well as earlier resolution of symptoms. A disadvantage of early surgery is that the condition may subsequently resolve spontaneously, thus treating more infants who may have not required surgery. A procedure is more painful in an awake infant and less controlled than under general anesthesia in an operating room.

question: A patient comes to the emergency department after being hit on the left side of the head with a baseball. He reports a progressive decrease in vision in the left eye. On examination, the globe is intact, the eyelids are tense, the intraocular pressure is elevated, there are pulsations of the central retinal artery, and a left aﬀerent pupillary defect is present. explanation: The situation described is concerning for an orbital compartment syndrome (OCS) from retrobulbar hemorrhage. The presence of an optic neuropathy and retinal arterial pulsations point to decreased perfusion to the globe and optic nerve and require emergency intervention. The most expeditious method to decompress the orbital soft tissue compartment is to perform lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis. It is critical to remember that OCS is a clinical diagnosis. A CT of the orbits often delays deﬁnitive treatment and should only be obtained once the cantholysis has been performed and the OCS reversed. question: What is the most common clinical feature of thyroid eye disease (TED)?
explanation: Eyelid retraction is the most common ophthalmic feature of TED, being present either unilaterally or bilaterally in more than 90% of patients at some point in their clinical course. Exophthalmos of one or both eyes aﬀects approximately 60% of patients, restrictive extraocular myopathy is apparent in about 40% of patients, and optic nerve dysfunction occurs in one or both eyes in approximately 5% of patients with TED. Only 5% of patients have the complete constellation of classic ﬁndings: eyelid retraction, exophthalmos, optic nerve dysfunction, extraocular muscle involvement, and hyperthyroidism. Upper eyelid retraction, either unilateral or bilateral, is documented in approximately 75% of patients at the time of diagnosis of TED. Lid lag in downgaze also is a frequent early sign, being present either unilaterally or bilaterally in 50% of patients at the initial examination. The most frequent ocular symptom when TED is ﬁrst conﬁrmed is dull, deep orbital pain or discomfort, which aﬀects 30% of patients. Some degree of diplopia is reported by approximately 17% of patients, lacrimation or photophobia by 15%–20% of patients, and blurred vision by 7% of patients. Decreased vision attributable to optic neuropathy is present in less than 2% of eyes at the time of diagnosis of TED. Pretibial myxedema and acropachy (soft-tissue swelling and periosteal changes aﬀecting the distal extremities, principally ﬁngers and toes) accompany TED in approximately 4% and 1% of patients, respectively, and are associated with a poor prognosis for the orbitopathy. Myasthenia gravis occurs in less than 1% of patients.

question: What branch of the facial nerve most commonly innervates the corrugator supercilii muscle?
explanation: The facial nerve divides into 5 branches. From superior to inferior, they are: temporal (frontal), zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The temporal (frontal) branch innervates the superior part of the facial mimetic muscles, including the corrugator supercilii.

question: What orbital inﬂammatory disease commonly aﬀects the respiratory system and kidneys?
explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis) is a necrotizing small-vessel granulomatous vasculitis of unknown etiology, classically aﬀecting the upper and lower respiratory system and the kidneys. Upper respiratory symptoms include sinusitis, chronic sinusitis, otitis, epistaxis, and ulcerations of the nasal mucosa. Lower respiratory symptoms include cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, pleurisy, and cavitary pneumonitis. Renal symptoms may be limited to microscopic hematuria. Other symptoms include arthralgia, fever, malaise, and weight loss. Idiopathic orbital inﬂammation (pseudotumor) sometimes occurs after upper respiratory infection, especially in children, but is otherwise not typically associated with systemic involvement. Sarcoidosis most commonly aﬀects the lungs, but the orbit may be aﬀected. Although sarcoidosis may aﬀect any organ system, renal involvement is not a common presentation.

question: Floppy eyelid syndrome is associated with what condition?
explanation: Floppy eyelid syndrome is characterized by a chronic papillary conjunctivitis, with ﬂaccid upper eyelids that evert easily. question: Incomplete development of what structure accounts for most cases of nasolacrimal duct blockage in infants?
explanation: The valve of Hasner, at the distal end of the nasolacrimal duct, under the inferior turbinate, is the last part of the duct to develop. question: A patient presents with intermittent diplopia that changes in every clinic visit and variable amounts of ptosis. What is the target of the antibody responsible for this condition?
explanation: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease characterized by antibody production against the acetylcholine receptor on the motor end plate of the muscle. Serologic testing for MG typically involves obtaining acetylcholine receptor antibodies, of which there are 3 types: blocking, binding, and modulating, named after their perceived mechanism of action. The ﬁrst 2 antibody tests are the more important. The remaining 3 answer choices (antibodies to acetylcholine, thyroid-stimulating antibodies, and ﬁbroblast growth factor receptor) do not ﬁt for MG. However, there is a known association between MG and thyroid dysfunction, and the thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) test, along with more conventional tests for thyroid abnormality, are sometimes ordered in patients with MG. question: A breast cancer patient is being treated with docetaxel. For 2 months, she has had tearing with epiphora. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

question: A patient presents with a left medial lower lid lesion consistent with an ulcerative basal cell carcinoma (Figure 1 Figure 1). What is the preferred management strategy for basal cell carcinomas in the medial canthal area adjacent to or surrounding the lacrimal outﬂow system?

explanation: When basal cell carcinomas involve the medial canthal area, the lacrimal drainage system may be excised in order to completely eradicate the tumor. If the lacrimal drainage system has been removed, reconstruction of the lacrimal outﬂow system is not undertaken until it is established that the patient is tumor free. Radiation therapy should also be considered only as a palliative treatment that should generally be avoided for periorbital lesions. In particular, it should not be used for canthal lesions, because there is a risk of orbital recurrence. As with cryotherapy, histologic margins cannot be evaluated, and the recurrence rate is higher after radiation treatment than after surgical treatment. Moreover, recurrence after radiation is more diﬃcult to detect, occurs at a longer interval after initial treatment, and is more challenging to manage surgically because of the altered healing of previously irradiated tissues. Complications of radiation therapy include cicatricial changes in the eyelids, lacrimal drainage scarring with obstruction, keratitis sicca, and radiation-induced malignancy.

question: What type of organism most often causes adult orbital cellulitis?
explanation: Infectious orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. The vast majority of cases are caused by bacterial sinusitis. In a young child, the maxillary and frontal sinuses are underdeveloped. Therefore, orbital cellulitis is most likely to arise from the ethmoidal sinus. In addition, the lamina papyracea is thin, and veins connect the ethmoid sinus to the orbit. In adults, infections are usually polymicrobial, including gram-positive cocci, Moraxella, and H. inﬂuenzae. However in children, the causative agent is usually a single organism that is typically a gram-positive organism. Adults often require early surgical intervention, whereas children typically improve with intravenous antibiotics alone.

question: During a direct brow lift, trauma to what nerve would likely cause tingling pain on the scalp?

question: A 76-year-old woman presents for evaluation of bilateral droopy upper lids. She has a 30-year history of bilateral hard contact lens use. She has good levator function, thin eyelid skin, and a high lid crease. What is the most likely explanation for her eyelid ptosis?
explanation: Characteristics of aponeurotic ptosis include older age, long- standing hard contact lens use, good levator function, thin eyelid skin, and a high lid crease. Additional history that may be associated with aponeurotic ptosis includes post-trauma, long- standing edema as in thyroid-related orbitopathy and blepharochalasis, and chronic allergies, with associated eye- rubbing. Neurogenic ptosis, such as Horner syndrome or cranial nerve (CN) III palsy, is often associated with other clinical ﬁndings, including pupillary changes. Previously unrecognized congenital ptosis does not usually have normal levator function. Acquired myogenic ptosis is uncommon and results from localized or diﬀuse muscular disease such as muscular dystrophy, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myasthenia gravis, or oculopharyngeal dystrophy. Mechanical ptosis usually refers to the condition in which an eyelid or orbital mass weighs or pulls down the upper eyelid, resulting in inferior displacement. It may be caused by a congenital abnormality, such as a plexiform neuroﬁbroma or hemangioma, or by an acquired neoplasm, such as a large chalazion or skin carcinoma. Postsurgical or posttraumatic edema may also cause temporary mechanical ptosis.

question: What location of a periocular lymphoma is associated with the lowest risk of systemic lymphomas?
explanation: It is important to understand the risk of systemic lymphoma in a patient with periocular lymphoma. More than half of periocular lymphomas involve prior, concurrent, or future systemic spread (20%-30% have previous or concomitant systemic disease, 30% develop it over 5 years). This risk is somewhat predicted by the site of periocular origin: The risk is lowest for conjunctival lesions, greater for orbital lesions and highest for eyelid lesions. Lesions in the lacrimal fossa may carry a greater risk than those occurring elsewhere in the orbit. Bilateral periocular involvement greatly increases the risk of systemic disease, but it is not a deﬁnitive sign of systemic disease. The risk of systemic disease is increased for decades after the original lesion is diagnosed, regardless of the initial lesion’s location. The prediction of biologic behavior of periorbital lymphoproliferative lesions is limited, despite clinical, histopathologic, and immunohistochemical studies. Pathologically, lymphoproliferative lesions with lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, a polymorphous mixture of plasma cells, and mature lymphocytes favor a diagnosis of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. More monotonous, small, round lymphocytes are seen in low-grade malignant lymphomas, whereas high-grade lymphomas demonstrate more malignant nuclei and frequent mitoses. explanation: An involutional punctal ectropion is most easily treated by a localized shortening of the posterior lamella. Because the tarsus tapers medially and laterally, very little if any tarsus is present near the punctum. Therefore, the posterior lamella in this area consists of conjunctiva alone. By excising a horizontal ellipse of tissue and then closing it, the posterior lamella is eﬀectively shortened, and the eyelid will rotate inward. Skin grafting (ie, lengthening of the anterior lamella) is an eﬀective treatment for a cicatricial ectropion from scarring, for example, but is not indicated in involutional cases. question: A child presents for a second opinion for chronic follicular conjunctivitis recalcitrant to topical steroids and antibiotics. The ophthalmologist notes a 2- mm skin-colored, domeshaped mass on the eyelid margin with a central small crater. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Molluscum contagiosum aﬀects primarily children 1 year to 10 years of age, but adults may be infected from exposure to lesions, especially through sexual activity or if immunodeﬁcient. The virus spreads from close contact (children at play, wrestling, sexual contact) or from scratching the nodules or coming in contact with fomites directly or through towels, communal baths, or tattoo instruments. The lesions typically last 6 to 8 weeks. Any area of skin may be aﬀected, usually torso or limbs but occasionally eyelids. The lesions are single or multiple ﬂesh- colored, opalescent, and domeshaped, measuring 1 to 5 mm in diameter. A central depressed crater develops with a waxy core. The eyelid margin location may be associated with unilateral, chronic follicular conjunctivitis. Multiple molluscum lesions in an adult should prompt consideration of HIV/AIDS. In contrast to other pox viruses, necrosis at the site of the lesion usually does not occur. Molluscum "bodies" can be demonstrated by smearing a glass slide with the material expressed from the central crater and examination with Giemsa, Gram-Wright, or Papanicolaou stains. Minor trauma (expression of the core, curettage, cryotherapy) often leads to regression. Eyelid margin lesions (usually single) may be removed by excisional biopsy and submitted for standard histopathologic diagnosis. This is usually curative for molluscum-associated follicular conjunctivitis. Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a DNA pox virus (molluscum contagiosum virus-MCV). The virus has 4 subtypes (MCV 1-4), with MCV-1 most prevalent, but with geographic variation. MCV infects all layers of the epithelium, multiplying in the cytoplasm of squamous cells, eventually creating a central crater ﬁlled with debris, which includes viable, contagious viral particles that are easily shed or abraded. Pathologic ﬁndings are marked thickening of the squamous layer of the epithelium, forming expanded, localized intraepidermal nodules. The squamous cells are ﬁlled with granular material (MCV particles), which replaces the cytoplasm and compresses the nucleus, forming molluscum inclusions. Orbital compartment syndrome (OCS) may occur in a variety of settings (eg, posttraumatic or postsurgical hemorrhage, abscess formation, noninfectious inﬂammation). Posttraumatic OCS usually results from hemorrhage. Large orbital fractures expand the orbital compartment into the adjacent paranasal sinuses, and this may be relatively protective against the development of OCS. However, if bleeding continues, blood will ﬁll this larger compartment, resulting in OCS. Therefore, it is important not to discount the possibility of OCS in patients with orbital fractures. Prompt lateral canthotomy and cantholysis should be performed by the emergency department physician, particularly if the ophthalmologist is not able to perform the procedure in a timely fashion. Inadequate cantholysis will not relieve the OCS, and complete release should be veriﬁed once the ophthalmologist has arrived. Conservative management with IV ﬂuids and pain management will only mask the pain noted in OCS. OCS is a clinical entity that can result in permanent visual loss if diagnosis is delayed. Therefore, deﬁnitive management should not be delayed by waiting for CT. OCS rarely manifests as a discrete hematoma on CT, but rather appears as an increased reticular signal in the intraconal fat. Posterior globe tenting may be seen on axial and parasagittal images, because the posterior sclera is distorted by proptosis and a stretched optic nerve. Bony orbital decompression is rarely needed in a patient with OCS. Use of intravenous mannitol may temporarily stabilize the OCS. If the OCS has not resolved, orbital surgery may be required.

question: What condition is likely to present with a palpable, smooth, painless mass in the superolateral orbit with pulsating proptosis upon mastication?
explanation: Orbital dermoids present as palpable, smooth, painless, ovoid masses that enlarge slowly. They are either freely mobile or adhere to the underlying periosteum. question: A mother is concerned that her newborn baby does not produce tears when he cries. The ophthalmologist reassures her and explains that the lacrimal gland is not yet fully developed. At approximately what age will the baby’s lacrimal gland be fully developed?

question: The lateral canthal tendon attaches to what structure?

question: What physical ﬁnding should prompt consideration of a pretrichial approach for brow lift surgery?

question: When repairing a deep upper eyelid laceration with fat in the wound, it is generally advisable to avoid suturing what structure?
explanation: An upper eyelid laceration with fat in the wound describes an injury where the orbital septum is involved. question: What is the most common form of basal cell carcinoma?

question: What upper eyelid mass most commonly causes mechanical ptosis?

Causes include plexiform neuroma, hemangioma, chalazion, skin carcinoma, orbital mass, and postsurgical or post-traumatic edema. question: Pulsatile exophthalmos is most closely associated with what neuro- oculocutaneous disorder?

question: In the emergency department following a motor vehicle accident, a patient has a normal globe examination and some periorbital ecchymosis, but no displacement of lateral canthus or malar ﬂattening. He denies any trismus. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a nondisplaced zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture. What management is recommended?
explanation: A zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture (ie, malar complex fracture) is a relatively frequent midfacial fracture pattern that typically involves 3 facial buttresses: the zygoma (typically along the lateral orbital wall at the level of the frontozygomatic suture), the zygomatic arch, and either the medial or lateral malar buttress extending to involve the inferior orbital rim. Not infrequently, the orbital ﬂoor is also fractured. Clinical problems occur for patients if the fractured complex rotates. This typically results in inferior lateral canthal dystopia, a step- oﬀ deformity along the inferior orbital rim, malar ﬂattening, and trismus (limitation of mandibular opening from impingement on the muscles of mastication by the displaced zygomatic arch). Once enough rotation occurs, repair is indicated. However, observation is all that is needed in cases of nondisplaced or minimally displaced tripod fractures. High-dose corticosteroids are not indicated in facial fractures, especially if concomitant intracranial injury exists. In this case, there is minimal soft tissue edema, and even normal doses of steroids would provide little, if any, beneﬁt. It is also important to remember that displaced (rotated) ZMC fractures are notorious for "hiding" or minimizing the extent of the orbital ﬂoor defect, so the orbital ﬂoor fracture tends to look much smaller than it actually is. However, once the ZMC is rotated and plated back into its native position, the ﬂoor defect will open more widely, expanding the orbital volume and potentially causing posttraumatic enophthalmos or hypoglobus. It is therefore prudent to explore the orbital ﬂoor defect once the ZMC has been rotated back into normal position, and, as necessary, to repair the ﬂoor appropriately.

question: A patient with mild seventh nerve dysfunction that began immediately after acoustic neuroma removal now has tearing. What is the most likely cause?

explanation: The seventh cranial nerve is often damaged during removal of an acoustic neuroma, resulting in partial or complete paralysis of the ipsilateral facial muscles of expression. Orbicularis weakness interferes with the normal lacrimal pump function, causing epiphora. Recurrence of the tumor would not be expected to cause tearing. Aberrant regeneration of the seventh cranial nerve could cause hyperlacrimation, but this is much less common, and it would not be expected immediately after surgery. Nasolacrimal duct obstruction can cause tearing, but it is unrelated to the clinical scenario described.

question: What orbital disorder demonstrates a ﬂuid-ﬂuid level with neuroimaging?
explanation: Previously termed lymphangiomas, lymphatic malformations result from aberrant development and congenital malformation of vessels. The classic ﬂuid-ﬂuid level on orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is seen with the so-called "chocolate cyst" of lymphatic malformations. Lymphatic malformations are relatively static lesions with very slow growth over time. The tumor becomes symptomatic when spontaneous bleeding occurs within its lymphatic channels, typically presenting as an acute orbitopathy. Bleeding sometimes occurs during or following upper respiratory infections and may be related to increased lymphocytic activity within the lesion, although this is admittedly conjecture. As the blood cyst matures and blood breakdown products form, a separation occurs between methemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin as a ﬂuid-ﬂuid level that is best seen on MRI and is sometimes compared to the oil-vinegar line of salad dressing. Blood cysts are not a feature of the remaining lesions. Cavernous hemangioma usually demonstrates a heterogeneous uptake of contrast on MRI, but this is markedly distinct from the ﬂuid-ﬂuid line of lymphatic malformations.

question: What historical characteristic of a lacrimal gland tumor is most suggestive of adenoid cystic carcinoma?

question: Lower eyelid retractor repair (reattachment) is most appropriate for correction of what condition?
explanation: The lower lid retractor muscles include the capsulopalpebral fascia and the inferior tarsal muscle. Reinsertion of the lower lid retractors is performed to repair involutional entropion. In addition to reinsertion of the lower lid retractors, partial myectomy of the preseptal orbicularis oculi muscle can be performed, as well as tightening of the lower lid by a lateral tarsal strip. These procedures address the 3 principal mechanisms behind involutional entropion: 1) horizontal laxity of the eyelid, 2) disinsertion or atrophy of the lower lid retractor complex, or 3) overriding preseptal orbicularis oculi muscle. In contrast, cicatricial entropion repair requires addressing the underlying problem (eg, controlling inﬂammation, autoimmune reaction, infection, or trauma) and using a graft to lengthen the posterior lamella.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is the most common malignant epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland. This highly malignant carcinoma may cause pain because of perineural invasion and bone destruction. The relatively rapid course, with a history of generally less than 1 year, and early onset of pain help diﬀerentiate ACC from pleomorphic adenoma, which is painless and characteristically exhibits progressive proptosis for more than a year. The tumor usually extends into the posterior orbit because of its capacity to inﬁltrate and its lack of true encapsulation. Most lacrimal gland masses represent nonspeciﬁc inﬂammation (dacryoadenitis). They present with acute inﬂammatory signs and usually respond to anti-inﬂammatory medication. They do not cause bony destruction or exhibit perineural invasion. The vast majority of orbital lymphoproliferative lesions are non- Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). The typical lymphoproliferative lesion presents as a gradually progressive, painless mass, resulting in proptosis, a visible periocular mass, or ptosis. These tumors are often located anteriorly in the orbit or beneath the conjunctiva, where they may show the typical salmon-patch appearance. Lymphoproliferative lesions, whether benign or malignant, usually mold to surrounding orbital structures rather than invade them; consequently, disturbances of extraocular motility or visual function are unusual.

question: Medial canthal reconstructions should be attached to what structure in order to maintain globe apposition?

question: What surgical approach is preferred for a suspected tumor in the lacrimal gland region?

question: What type of foreign body could be followed with observation and without surgery when located deep in the orbit?
explanation: Because a bullet enters the orbit at high velocity (and therefore high temperature), it may be considered a sterile foreign body. The projectile portion (as opposed to the casing) is typically made of an alloy containing a variety of metals, including copper, steel, aluminum, and bronze. This combination is usually (but not always) nonreactive in orbital soft tissue. It is reasonable to leave in place a bullet fragment that is deep in the orbit as long as it is not causing a compressive optic neuropathy. Copper often induces a signiﬁcant inﬂammatory reaction in the orbit and should be removed. Both copper and iron can also have a chronic toxic eﬀect on the eye: chalcosis and siderosis bulbi, respectively.

explanation: The lacrimal sac ductules consist of 2 to 6 ductules that extend from the orbital lobe of the lacrimal gland, into the palpebral lobe, and join the palpebral lobe ducts. From there, 8 to 12 major palpebral lobe ductules drain into the lateral superior fornix cul- de-sac. They are located 4-5 mm above the superior margin of the upper tarsus. The lateral horn inserts onto the lateral orbital tubercle, and it divides the lacrimal gland into orbital and palpebral lobes, attaching ﬁrmly to the orbital tubercle. The lacrimal artery lies within the stroma of the lacrimal gland and is unlikely to be injured during surgery within the conjunctival cul-de-sac.

question: Biopsy of a lacrimal gland mass via the palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland risks damage to what structure?
explanation: The lacrimal gland is divided into orbital and palpebral lobes by indentation from the lateral horn of the levator aponeurosis. Lacrimal excretory ducts pass through the palpebral portion of the gland, so removal of, or damage to (by biopsy), the palpebral portion of the gland can severely reduce secretion from the lacrimal gland. The accessory lacrimal glands are located in the superior fornix (Krauss) and superior border of the tarsus (Wolfring). The origin of the lacrimal artery is the ophthalmic artery, which is not near the palpebral lobe. The eﬀerent nerve supply to the lacrimal gland is by way of parasympathetic ﬁbers from cranial nerve VII in the greater superﬁcial petrosal nerve, which sends ﬁbers to the sphenopalatine ganglion, and then by way of the zygomatic nerve.

question: What is a contraindication to evisceration?
explanation: The potential for sympathetic ophthalmia is a common admonition against evisceration and for enucleation. In fact, sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare event, and no deﬁnitive correlation with evisceration has been proved (although some anecdotal evidence does exist). The most ominous risk of evisceration is an occult intraocular malignancy; evisceration would allow spillage of tumor out of the eye. Because of this possibility, evisceration should not be performed without a detailed view of the fundus.

question: What is the most common presentation of rhabdomyosarcoma?
explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary orbital malignancy of childhood. The average age of onset is 5–7 years. The classic clinical picture is that of a child with sudden onset and rapid progression of unilateral proptosis. However, patients in their early teens may experience a less dramatic course, with gradually progressive proptosis developing over weeks to more than a month. There is often a marked adnexal response with edema and discoloration of the eyelids. Ptosis and strabismus may also be present. A mass may be palpable, particularly in the superonasal quadrant of the eyelid, and it may cause proptosis if suﬃciently large. However, the tumor may be retrobulbar, may involve any quadrant of the orbit, and may in rare cases arise from the conjunctiva. Although pain is an occasional complaint, it is seen in only a minority of rhabdomyosarcoma cases. Optic neuropathy is uncommon in rhabdomyosarcoma unless the tumor is allowed to progress without timely diagnosis and treatment.

explanation: Nasoethmoidal complex (NEC) fractures often result in rounding of the medial canthal angle and lacrimal drainage injury. In most cases, the medial canthal tendon (MCT) attachments to bone remain intact, but the MCT is incorrectly positioned because of the displaced bone fragment. The main diﬃculty in MCT repositioning in NEC fractures is obtaining the correct posterior vector. Anatomically, the MCT consists of 2 limbs (anterior and posterior), which splay around the lacrimal sac and attach to their respective lacrimal crests. The key to MCT reconstruction is the posterior lacrimal crest attachment; more anterior attachment of the MCT will result in medial ectropion. Not infrequently, the posterior lacrimal crest is involved in the NEC fracture and is unstable. The posterior lacrimal crest positioning of the MCT must therefore be achieved through other means. If the underlying bone of the NEC fracture is not stable, transnasal wiring will not work: The wire will simply migrate anteriorly because of inadequate bony support. One eﬀective method for MCT reconstruction in NEC fracture is to cantilever a miniplate posteriorly into the medial orbit from stable anterior nasal bone. One of the holes of the miniplate serves as an anchor for the MCT repair. Lacrimal drainage injury is also common in NEC fractures, but routine intubation is usually not recommended. Intubation may be unnecessary and is often diﬃcult because of soft tissue swelling and underlying fracture; attempted intubation may result in a false passage of the tubes and further injury to the lacrimal sac or nasolacrimal duct. If lacrimal obstruction occurs from the NEC fracture, it can be repaired at a later date with dacryocystorhinostomy.

A dacryocystocele occurs when mucus is trapped in the tear sac because of a functional block above the sac (valve of Rosenmüller) and obstruction at the distal end (valve of Hasner) of the NLD. The dacryocystocele is initially sterile and may respond to conservative management with prophylactic topical antibiotics and digital compression of the lacrimal sac. When there is minimal improvement or infection develops, probing of the lacrimal drainage system may be necessary to address the disorder. Extension of the dacryocystocele cyst into the nasal cavity at the level of an occluded valve of Hasner may also occur. Intranasal examination and urgent treatment are needed if the condition is bilateral and causes airway obstruction, as infants are obligate nasal breathers. question: What type of tumor is an orbital dermoid?
explanation: Dermoid and epidermoid cysts are among the most common benign orbital tumors of childhood. These cysts are present congenitally and enlarge progressively. The more superﬁcial cysts usually become symptomatic in childhood, but deeper orbital dermoids may not become clinically evident until adulthood. Both dermoid and epidermoid cysts are lined by keratinizing epithelium; however, dermoids may contain dermal appendages such as hair follicles and sebaceous glands, while epidermoids do not. Both epidermoids and dermoids represent choristomas. These are tissue anomalies characterized by normal cells that are not normally found at the involved site. Other choristomas include dermolipomas and teratomas. Hamartomas are anomalous growths of tissue consisting only of mature cells that are normally found at the involved site. Examples of these are infantile (capillary) hemangiomas and the characteristic lesions of neuroﬁbromatosis.

explanation: The ﬁgure shows entrapment of the left medial rectus muscle in a left medial orbital wall fracture. Clinically, the patient has pain and restriction on abduction in conjunction with nausea and emesis. In this setting, urgent surgical intervention is indicated. Sometimes, a trial of steroids with close observation for 24 hours may be indicated prior to surgical intervention. However, ongoing ischemia to an entrapped rectus muscle may lead to loss of function if release of the muscle is not performed in a timely manner. Forced duction testing determines whether an ocular motility dysfunction is a restrictive or paretic process. The test is performed by ﬁrst applying topical anesthesia to the eye. Then forceps are used to grasp the Tenon capsule and conjunctiva near the limbus and passively move the eye. With an acute entrapment of the medial rectus muscle, a restriction in abduction of the eye would be anticipated. There may also be restriction with adduction of the eye. Forced generation testing determines the active force produced by the extraocular muscles. After topical anesthesia is applied, the examiner grasps the Tenon capsule and conjunctiva near the limbus. The examiner then asks the patient to attempt an eye movement, and the force generated by the extraocular muscle is observed. Patients with paretic muscles have reduced forced generations. In a patient with an entrapped medial rectus muscle, reduced forced generation may be observed with adduction if the medial rectus is injured. However, forced generation with abduction should be normal, since the lateral rectus appears uninjured.

question: When removing bone from the medial wall in an orbital decompression, where can the surgeon locate the posterior ethmoidal arteries?
explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries are critical anatomic landmarks to identify during orbital decompression. Their foramina both lie along the line of the frontoethmoidal suture (FES). The FES usually deﬁnes the level of the cribriform plate and fovea ethmoidalis, which separate the skull base from the ethmoid sinuses. As a general statement, penetration of the medial wall below this level is safe, because it decompresses the orbit into the sinuses; penetration of the orbit above this level is fraught with potential neurologic complications, since the surgeon would enter the intracranial space. That said, many pathologic conditions (craniofacial anomalies such as Crouzon syndrome, etc.) are characterized by a low-lying skull base, and not infrequently, otherwise normal patients will present with a low skull base; review of preoperative imaging is therefore crucial in all patients.

The upper eyelid defect shown in the ﬁgure is best repaired with what surgical procedure? Cutaneous malignant melanomas of the eyelids are rare. They may develop de novo or from a pre-existing nevus. Clinically, invasive melanoma is often preceded by a vertical growth phase, resulting in an elevated, indurated mass. Histologic features suggesting malignancy include nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli, or atypical mitotic ﬁgures. Melanoma invades the epidermis and lacks the polarity found in melanocytic nevi. There are 4 main histologic subtypes of dermal melanoma. The superﬁcial spreading variant is the most common type of cutaneous melanoma. It demonstrates a spreading intraepidermal growth pattern. The lentigo maligna subtype is the most common cutaneous melanoma aﬀecting the eyelids. It has a long pre-invasive phase, and carries the best prognosis. It appears histologically as a nest or line of atypical melanocytes, predominantly in the basal layers of the epidermis. Acral lentiginous melanoma involves the extremities and is not found on the eyelids. Nodular melanoma is histologically characterized by a minimal intraepidermal component and more pronounced vertical growth, making it more deeply invasive. It carries the worst prognosis.

With trauma, there is rarely tissue loss and therefore, primary closure of tarsus, subcutaneous tissue, and skin is the surgical procedure of choice. question: An ophthalmologist is called to evaluate a patient in the emergency department who was transferred from another hospital. The patient has had progressive swelling of the right eyelid for the past several days. He has also had fevers, malaise, anorexia, and altered mental status. On examination, he has pronounced violaceous swelling of the right orbit, with areas of necrosis. The orbit is tight and requires immediate canthotomy/cantholysis. The right pupil is amaurotic and vision in that eye is no light perception (NLP). His left eye has a reactive pupil with vision of 20/25. Blood cultures sent from the outside hospital are positive for Group A beta hemolytic streptococcus. What is the next step in management?
