explanation: The photo and clinical presentation are concerning for necrotizing fasciitis (NF). Given the high mortality rate, and the fact that NF patients can clinically decline very rapidly, all patients with NF should be admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for monitoring, as opposed to a general medical ﬂoor. Although starting immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics is a correct measure to take, plans to go to the operating room (OR) should not be delayed to watch for improvement. Prompt surgical treatment is one of the most important factors to decrease mortality in NF. This patient should be taken to the OR to debride necrotic tissue as expeditiously as possible (ideally within no more than a few hours of presentation). Group A beta hemolytic streptococcus is the usual culprit in the etiology of NF. The aggressive nature of NF is determined in large part by how invasive that particular strain of the bacteria is. Virulence factors for this bacteria include the M protein and pyrogenic exotoxins (not endotoxins). M protein is an antiphagocytic virulence factor that renders the bacteria resistant to attack by host leukocytes. Pyrogenic exotoxins that are released cause fever, shock, and widespread tissue injury, potentially precipitating multiorgan failure. Although risk factors for necrotizing fasciitis include conditions that can cause some degree of immunosuppression (diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, malignancy, rheumatologic disease), one study showed that 52% of NF patients were healthy and had no risk factors. Therefore, patients with NF do not automatically warrant an immunosuppressive workup or HIV screening. NF has also been reported following minor trauma (including after blepharoplasty and dacryocystorhinostomy [DCR] procedures).

question: An otherwise healthy 12-year- old boy with no prior ocular history presents to the oﬃce for an eye examination. He has a pattern of incomplete hair loss on the scalp. The remaining hairs on his scalp have variable length. He is also missing hair from part of his left eyebrow. explanation: The patient presents with trichotillomania. This disorder is seen most commonly in patients aged 9 to 13 years old. It is characterized by the compulsive urge to pull out one’s own hair. Typically the patient presents with hair loss on the scalp or eyebrows or eyelashes. The remaining hair on the scalp may have variable lengthens due to repeated hair removal. Stress is thought to be a precipitating factor. Consultation with a psychologist or psychiatrist to evaluate the causes of this behavior is the recommended treatment. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have risks that are beyond the scope of an ophthalmology visit, but may be eﬀective treatment. Atomoxetine (Strattera) is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor used to treat attention-deﬁcit hyperactivity disorder. question: A 61-year-old woman has noted slowly progressive painless visual loss OD over the last 6 months. Her visual acuity is 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS. The sagittal T1- weighted MRI with contrast and fat suppression shows fusiform enhancement of the superior optic nerve sheath (black arrow) and linear enhancement of the inferior optic nerve sheath (red arrowhead) in the right orbit with a thin nonenhancing optic nerve between the enhancing optic nerve sheath, consistent with an optic nerve sheath meningioma. Distensible venous malformations of the orbit, previously known as orbital varices, are best visualized with MRI or contrast- enhanced rapid spiral computed tomography (CT) during a Valsalva maneuver, showing characteristic enlargement of the engorged veins. Phleboliths may also be present on imaging. Cavernous venous malformations, previously known as cavernous hemangiomas, are the most common primary orbital lesion in adults which are described as a well-circumscribed (not fusiform) lesion within the muscle cone that may have heterogenous enhancement. Optic nerve gliomas are very rare in adults (more common in children) and are best visualized with MRI as a heterogenous mass in the orbital apex with fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve (not the optic nerve sheath).

question: During conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR), where is a Jones tube best positioned?
explanation: Positioning and angulation of a Jones tube are critical for its success. A CDCR bypasses the lacrimal anatomy and allows tears to drain directly from the lids and eye into the nasal cavity via capillary action of the glass Jones tube. The lacrimal sac is normally found along the anterior aspect of the middle meatus and extends superiorly to the root of the middle turbinate. The Jones tube passes through the lacrimal sac and, similarly to a dacryocystorhinostomy, passes through a surgical osteotomy in the medial wall of the sac and lateral wall of the nasal cavity. Positioning the Jones tube just anterior to the middle turbinate provides the correct angulation for tear drainage. The valve of Hasner is located in the inferior meatus, beneath the inferior turbinate. It would be extremely diﬃcult to position the tip of the Jones tube in this location because of the length, amount of bone, and acute angulation.

question: A 44-year-old woman presents with gradually progressive proptosis of the right eye without visual loss or diplopia but accompanied by a dull aching retrobulbar pain. On examination, she has mild proptosis that signiﬁcantly increases with Valsalva maneuver. What orbital lesion is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Proptosis that increases when a patient’s head is dependent or after a Valsalva maneuver suggests the presence of a venous malformation. Venous malformations of the orbit are known as orbital varices, which are low-ﬂow vascular lesions. At rest, these patients may exhibit enophthalmos, as the varix is not engorged. Diagnosis of these lesions can be conﬁrmed with a contrast- enhanced rapid spiral computed tomography (CT) during a Valsalva maneuver. Cavernous hemangiomas, the most common benign neoplasm of the orbit in adults, can also present with proptosis, but this is a slowly progressive proptosis and does not change with pressure dependence or Valsalva. Hemangiopericytomas are uncommon and can resemble cavernous hemangiomas on radiologic imaging, but these tumors also do not vary in size with Valsalva. Neurilemomas, also known as schwannomas, are proliferations of Schwann cells encapsulated by perineurium.

By contrast, patients with signiﬁcant involutional changes, including medial and lateral canthal laxity, can often undergo direct closure for defects involving up to one-third of the eyelid. In this case, a lateral canthal release should provide enough laxity to advance the intact lateral eyelid as a full-thickness ﬂap to close the defect, and it is the easiest solution, using only 1 step.

question: What cutaneous malignancy is associated with actinic keratosis?
explanation: Actinic keratosis is the most common precancerous skin lesion, often aﬀecting people with fair complexion and a history of chronic sun exposure. Over extended follow-up, a patient with multiple actinic keratoses has a 12% to 20% incidence of squamous cell carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant neoplasm of the eyelid. question: A patient sustains a low transverse fracture in the maxilla above the teeth without any orbital involvement. What type of fracture is this?
explanation: Le Fort described a series of 3 facial fracture patterns following blunt trauma. Put simply, the fractures progress from the palate to the skull base across the medial buttresses of the face in a pyramidal fashion. A Le Fort I fracture is a transverse fracture of the maxilla just above the teeth and has no orbital involvement. A Le Fort II fracture involves the midface. It typically involves the maxilla and may extend to the lacrimal drainage system, resulting in posttraumatic epiphora. A Le Fort III fracture is most easily described as complete craniofacial disjunction: The fracture extends across both orbits and the skull base (involving the sphenoid bone). In short, the face is fractured away from its attachments to the skull. Le Fort III fractures may involve the optic canals and result in traumatic optic neuropathy. Naso-orbital ethmoidal or nasoethmoidal complex involve the bones in the area of the medial canthal tendon and lacrimal sac. They may result in telecanthus, medial canthal rounding, and epiphora. A zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture, also known as a tripod or cheekbone fracture, involves the horizontal and vertical buttresses of the maxilla and zygoma. The inferior and lateral orbital rims are usually involved, and an orbital ﬂoor fracture is an associated ﬁnding.

question: Bowen disease is a risk factor for the development of what type of invasive skin cancer?
explanation: Bowen disease refers to squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin. In 5% of patients, Bowen disease may progress to vertically invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Bowen disease is not related to the other types of skin cancer listed (basal cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma).

question: For 2 weeks, a patient has an edematous, erythematous lesion above the eyelid margin as shown. He had a similar lesion treated on the upper eyelid 2 years ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis in this clinical scenario is a chalazion. Basal cell and sebaceous gland carcinoma are less likely to present as an inﬂammatory process over a short period. A BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the best initial therapy for nonspeciﬁc orbital inﬂammation (NSOI)?
explanation: NSOI, formerly known as orbital pseudotumor or idiopathic orbital inﬂammatory syndrome, is a diagnosis of exclusion. For initial occurrences with typical clinical features, initial therapy is a trial of oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg/day. If there is complete clinical remission, the steroid is then slowly tapered. Incomplete response or recurrent inﬂammation should prompt biopsy.

question: What eyelid lesion is most appropriately managed with Mohs micrographic surgery?
explanation: Mohs micrographic surgery can be useful in the management of skin malignancy. Basal cell carcinoma is a perfect candidate for Mohs micrographic surgery because it exhibits contiguous spread without skip lesions or metastasis, and interpretation of the histopathology on frozen sections is reliable. Malignant melanoma and Merkel cell carcinoma require wide resection with BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What should the physician do during an epiphora evaluation after assessing for pseudoepiphora and as an initial step for evaluation of lacrimal outﬂow problems?

options.B: Evaluate the corneal and conjunctival epithelium.
options.C: Instill topical anesthetic in each eye and wait 30 seconds.
options.D: Observe the eyelid and puncta positions during the blink cycle.

explanation: Examination of a patient with epiphora starts by distinguishing between an etiology of hypersecretion and an etiology of lacrimal outﬂow obstruction. Pseudoepiphora evaluation includes assessment of the tear meniscus, tear breakup time, corneal and conjunctival epithelium, basal tear secretion (assessed with the use of topical anesthetic), and corneal irritation. Observation of the patient's eyelid and punctal positions during the blink cycle prior to manipulation of the lids is the ﬁrst step in evaluation for lacrimal outﬂow obstruction. Slit-lamp examination during the blink cycle allows for the determination of correct position of the punctum, weakened or incomplete blinks, poor lacrimal pump function, and mechanical blockage of the punctum as causes of epiphora. Performing lacrimal irrigation for evaluation of lacrimal outﬂow obstruction would be one diagnostic test in the evaluation of epiphora after the assessment of the blink dynamics.

question: An obese 27-year-old woman with headaches and horizontal diplopia presents to the clinic. After thorough evaluation and testing, the ophthalmologist diagnoses her with pseudotumor cerebri and begins treatment with acetazolamide. She promptly develops Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) with ocular involvement, requiring a prolonged hospital stay. question: After cosmetic blepharoplasty, a 45-year-old woman presents with bumps on one of the incisions. The bumps are smooth, round, and freely mobile. There is no erythema, edema, or tenderness. What is the likely mechanism of these lesions?
explanation: The answer is a common postoperative ﬁnding in patients undergoing upper eyelid blepharoplasty: iatrogenic inclusion cysts along the incision/suture line, known as epidermal inclusion cysts. When multiple tiny epidermal inclusion cysts are found, they are sometimes referred to as milia. In most cases, the lesions are small, resolve over time, and are "felt more than seen." Occasionally, larger milia may require excision. Whether or not speciﬁc suture material and technique increase the risk of milia formation is debatable. One additional entity for the surgeon to consider in a patient presenting with postoperative "bumps" along the incision line is infection. Typical bacterial infection usually presents with diﬀuse erythema and tenderness across the surgical site, and responds rapidly to oral antibiotics. However, on occasion a smoldering, minimally erythematous, minimally tender nodular process may manifest several weeks postoperatively. Fungal and atypical mycobacterial infection must be considered in such cases. A biopsy for histopathologic and microbacterial studies is usually required for the diagnosis.

question: Six months after enucleation, a patient returns to the oﬃce reporting mucoid discharge from the anophthalmic side. There is no pain. She states that the prosthesis ﬁts well. What is the most likely cause of the mucus discharge?
explanation: Chronic mucus discharge from an anophthalmic socket is usually due to a papillary conjunctivitis. This is due to mechanical friction between the palpebral conjunctival surface and the prosthesis. Everting the upper eyelid will demonstrate the papillary reaction. Treatment consists of topical corticosteroids and occasionally prosthetic modiﬁcation. Implant extrusion can present in a similar fashion, but it is less common than papillary conjunctivitis. The formation of a pyogenic granuloma is suggestive of an implant exposure. Implant infection is usually painful, and examination reveals BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient presents with progressive monocular vision loss. What is the most likely diagnosis? A palpable mass in the medial canthal area superior to the medial canthal tendon is suspicious for a lacrimal sac malignancy or a nonlacrimal-based mass such as a meningocele or mucocele. Distention of the lacrimal sac associated with chronic dacryocystitis would typically cause a palpable mass inferior to the medial canthal tendon. A lacrimal gland tumor would be located in the temporal aspect of the upper lid and superior orbit, not in the medial canthal area. While rare, lacrimal sac tumors are benign 45 of the time and malignant 55 of the time. Squamous cell papillomas and carcinomas are the most common tumors of the sac. A sphenoid wing meningioma would cause a mass in the temporal fossa.
explanation: Fibrous dysplasia is a bone tumor in which normal cancellous bone is replaced by immature woven bone and ﬁbrous cystic tissue. Involvement of the optic canal can lead to vision loss. Neuroﬁbromatosis is associated with absence of the sphenoid rim, but not bony tumors. Although osteomas are bone lesions with hyperostosis, they typically have well-deﬁned margins.

question: To avoid excessive skin removal during an upper lid blepharoplasty, a minimum of how much remaining skin is typically left between the inferior border of the brow and the upper eyelid margin? In this setting, zygomycosis (also termed phycomycosis or mucormycosis), which is the most common and devastating fungus of the orbit, is suspected. Patients present with an orbital apex syndrome with sinusitis. The fungus directly invades blood vessels, causing vessel thrombosis (even central retinal artery occlusion in rare cases). The tissue appears necrotic and a black eschar may be seen. Predisposing conditions include metabolic acidosis, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, organ transplantation, renal failure, immunosuppression, and malignancies (such as lymphoma/leukemia). Microscopically nonseptate, large branching hyphae that stain with hematoxylin and eosin (unlike most fungi) are seen. Treatment is aggressive surgical debridement with intravenous amphotericin B. Even with aggressive treatment, outcomes can be poor. Intravenous antibiotics such as vancomycin, nasal decongestants, and consultation with an otolaryngologist are indicated for possible MRSA, or orbital cellulitis not responding to oral antibiotics, but the symptoms, the predisposing factor of uncontrolled diabetes, and the presence of an eschar require more aggressive action.

question: The frontoethmoid suture is a clinically important landmark depicting the location of what structure?

options.A: superior aspect of the nasolacrimal fossa

explanation: The frontoethmoid suture runs along the border of the medial wall and the roof. It marks the approximate location of the cribriform plate, which is superior and medial to the frontoethmoid suture line. The frontoethmoid suture is also the site of the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries and veins. The nasolacrimal fossa along the medial wall is the attachment site of anterior and posterior limbs of medial canthal tendon. The ostium of the nasofrontal duct can be injured during frontal sinus fracture. The superior aspect of the nasolacrimal fossa houses the lacrimal sac.

question: A 38-year-old patient undergoes lateral orbitotomy to excise an intraconal cavernous hemangioma located in the inferior, posterior lateral orbit. The patient reports trouble reading. What is the most likely cause of the patient's postoperative reading diﬃculties?

options.A: hemorrhage within the optic nerve sheath
options.B: disruption of the posterior ciliary arteries

explanation: The ciliary ganglion is at risk for injury in lateral approaches to the intraconal space. The parasympathetic innervation, which controls accommodation and pupillary constriction, synapses within the ciliary ganglion. With injury to the ciliary ganglion, parasympathetic innervation is disrupted, causing postoperative accommodative diﬃculty.

question: A 7-year-old boy has had relapsing episodes of unilateral proptosis and swelling of the right superotemporal orbit unresponsive to oral antibiotics. Computed tomography (CT) scan reveals a lytic defect in the frontal bone. What is the next step in management?
explanation: Any orbital mass causing bony destruction raises concern for malignancy. The most common malignancies to consider in children are primary rhabdomyosarcoma, metastatic neuroblastoma, and granulocytic sarcoma. These 3 processes typically progress rapidly rather than having relapsing episodes as described in the stem. In addition to malignancy, a variety of histiocytic disorders that preferentially aﬀect children must be considered. Previously known as histiocytosis X, this group of disorders is now called Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). The most frequent presentation in the orbit is a lytic defect, usually aﬀecting the superotemporal orbit or sphenoid wing and causing relapsing episodes of orbital inﬂammation, often initially misinterpreted as infectious orbital cellulitis. Treatment of localized orbital disease consists of conﬁrmatory biopsy with debulking, which may be followed by intralesional steroid injection or low-dose radiation therapy. Children with systemic disease are treated aggressively with chemotherapy. No infection is present, so converting to intravenous antibiotics or performing incision and drainage is inappropriate. An empiric trial of corticosteroids is contraindicated because of the bone involvement—idiopathic orbital inﬂammatory syndrome does not cause bone destruction.

question: A 72-year-old man with a history of cancer is urgently referred to an ophthalmologist because of proptosis and orbital congestion of his left eye. On examination, no intraocular pathology is found. His vision, pupils, and intraocular pressure are normal. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a posterior orbital mass with sclerotic changes of the bone. What cancer is classically associated with this lesion?
explanation: Metastatic prostate cancer is classically associated with osteoblastic lesions. Lung cancer is the most frequent origin of orbital metastasis in men, and breast cancer is the most common in women. ALL is the most common leukemia to metastasize to BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 70-year-old woman presents with a left lower lid lesion. She has had multiple recurrent chalazia at the same location. Examination shows a yellowish lesion at the lid margin with loss of overlying eyelashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: system for the preseptal portion of the upper eyelid? ! " # sebaceous gland carcinoma

explanation: Sebaceous gland carcinomas are highly malignant tumors arising from sebaceous glands of the eyelid. These tumors may masquerade as recurrent chalazia or as chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis. More than 50% of cases are initially misdiagnosed. Because these lesions typically demonstrate pagetoid spread, wide excisional biopsy and map biopsy of the conjunctiva are typically required. Merkel cell carcinomas are typically violaceous-appearing lesions of the upper eyelid. These lesions are highly malignant and portend a poor prognosis. Oncocytomas are slow-growing cystadenomas arising from the ductal and acinar cells of the accessory and main lacrimal glands, and may present as reddish-brown caruncular lesions. Rosacea is characterized by excessive sebum secretion with frequently recalcitrant chronic blepharitis. It can progress, leading to chronic conjunctivitis, severe stromal keratitis, marginal keratitis, sterile ulceration, episcleritis, or iridocyclitis. If properly treated, these lesions can resolve with few sequelae.

question: What is the goal of treatment in a patient with severe microphthalmia?

options.A: functional vision in the microphthalmic eye

explanation: Microphthalmia with orbital cyst results from failure of the choroidal ﬁssure to close in the embryo. Because most microphthalmic eyes have no potential for vision, treatment focuses on achieving a cosmetically acceptable appearance that is reasonably symmetrical. Enucleation is usually not necessary for the ﬁtting of a conformer or prosthesis and is generally avoided. These cysts do not undergo malignant transformation. Mutations in ﬁbroblast growth factor receptor genes typically occur in syndromic craniosynostosis.

question: A 17-year-old trapeze artist has noticed increased left-sided, deep orbital pain and occasional loss of vision when performing upside down for a prolonged period of time. explanation: Gravity-dependent changes, which can be observed during examination, are most frequently secondary to orbital varices. These venous malformations are a result of vascular dysgenesis and are low-ﬂow vascular lesions, as opposed to arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), which are high-ﬂow anomalies. It is important to evaluate these patients with contrast-enhanced BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

A patient presents with a biopsy-proven, poorly diﬀerentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the medial canthus with aggressive growth. During deﬁnitive tumor extirpation, the medial canthus and canaliculi are removed. What would appropriate management include? &

options.A: anchoring medial canthal attachments of the remaining eyelid margin ﬁrmly to the periosteum or bone with dissolvable suture to prevent postoperative ectropion and granuloma formation

options.C: small margin excisions in order to minimize the degree of functional disruption to the surrounding tissues and lacrimal system
options.D: a glabellar or forehead ﬂap rotated to cover the defect

explanation: Repair of medial canthal defects is often diﬃcult because of the inherent complex 3-dimensional anatomy and the presence of the lacrimal drainage system. Since in this case the defect was created as a result of resection of a tumor, the patient may have to tolerate epiphora until recurrence of the tumor is no longer a risk. A glabellar or forehead rotational ﬂap is a reasonable option, with the understanding that such ﬂaps are often thick and may need subsequent debulking as a second stage procedure. When full-thickness medial eyelid defects are present, the medial canthal attachments of the remaining eyelid margin must be ﬁxed to ﬁrm periosteum or bone with heavy permanent suture, wire, or titanium miniplates. Until tumor recurrence is ruled out, it is critical to avoid lacrimal surgery that could create a pathway for the tumor to spread into the nose or sinuses. Lacrimal surgery may be performed several BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis for the eyelid lesion shown?
What type of secretion does a meibomian gland have? &

options.D: associated with the annulus of Zinn? ! " # eccrine aqueous secretion

explanation: Meibomian glands are modiﬁed sebaceous glands on the tarsus that have holocrine oily secretion. A holocrine gland forms the secretory product within the cytoplasm, and the secretion is released by the disruption of the plasma membrane and death of the cell. The glands of Zeis are located on the eyelid margin and are modiﬁed sebaceous glands that have holocrine oily secretion. Goblet cells also have holocrine mucus secretion. The glands of Krause and Wolfring are accessory lacrimal glands that have exocrine aqueous secretion. Exocrine glands secrete their product directly into the duct. The glands of Krause are located in the lateral part of the upper fornix. The glands of Wolfring are scattered along the proximal margin of tarsus. The glands of Moll are apocrine sweat glands, located near the eyelashes (cilia), that have eccrine secretion. An eccrine (or merocrine) gland is a sweat gland that produces water and sodium chloride that is secreted through exocytosis. An eccrine gland is composed of an intraepidermal spiral duct with a coiled acinar portion within the dermis. The glands of Moll are the only eccrine-secreting glands of the eyelid.

question: What osseous orbital feature is associated with the annulus of Zinn? eccrine aqueous secretion D.
explanation: The annulus of Zinn is a ﬁbrous structure in the apex of the orbit that is formed by the common origin of the 4 rectus muscles. It separates the superior orbital ﬁssure into 2 compartments, with associated nerves and blood vessels entering the orbit in a predictable fashion within these 2 spaces. The infraorbital ﬁssure, ethmoidal foramen, and inferior orbital groove are not associated with this structure. frontoethmoidal suture.

question: What cranial suture are orbital dermoid cysts most commonly adjacent to?
explanation: Orbital dermoid cysts are congenital choristomas lined by keratinized epithelium and dermal appendages (as opposed to epidermoid cysts, which are lined by only epidermis and do not contain dermal appendages). Usually recognized in childhood, they present as a mass in the superotemporal or superomedial quadrant of the orbit. Of the 2, the superotemporal quadrant along the frontozygomatic suture is most common. Less commonly, they may occur at the suture between the frontal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla. Dermoid cysts can be freely mobile or attached to the underlying periosteum.

question: What lid structure should be purposefully left open in a lid repair following penetrating trauma?
explanation: When perforated, the orbital septum should not be repaired, because this would inevitably cause horizontal scarring and shortening. Prolapsed fat can be repositioned, but the septum will close on its own during the healing process, and skin closure will usually hold prolapsed fat back. All of the other structures mentioned (the medial canthal tendon, levator aponeurosis, and lateral canthal tendon) must be assessed after orbital trauma. If injured, they must be reattached in order to restore support and functionality of the lids.

question: What is the most common additional disorder that an infant with congenital anophthalmos is at risk to develop?
explanation: Orbital bone growth is normally stimulated by the eye. In cases of microphthalmos or anophthalmos, it is common for the orbit to become hypoplastic compared to the non-aﬀected side over time. Enlarged socket and hyperplastic eyelids would not be expected. Ptosis can be seen in cases of anophthalmia, but not as commonly as the development of a hypoplastic orbit, which is the most common concern in this disorder.

question: In a patient with insidious onset of an esotropia and hypotropia associated with lid retraction, what is the most likely etiology of the ocular misalignment?
explanation: The restrictive strabismus of thyroid eye disease (TED) most often causes hypotropia and esotropia from involvement of the inferior and medial recti muscles, respectively. Eyelid retraction is the most common clinical feature of TED (present in more than 90% of patients at some point in their clinical course), and TED is the most common cause of eyelid retraction. A partial CN III palsy can cause ptosis and exotropia as well as hypotropia. Carotid cavernous ﬁstula can produce multiple cranial nerve palsies but not eyelid retraction. Orbital inﬂammatory syndrome usually has a more rapid course and almost always is painful.

question: A 70-year-old patient presents with slowly progressive unilateral ptosis with a high lid crease, a deep superior sulcus, and normal levator function. Following instillation of phenylephrine, his lid position does not change. What is the preferred method of ptosis repair? The etiology of orbital inﬂammation can be infectious, autoimmune, vasculitic, granulomatous, or nonspeciﬁc. This patient's inﬂammation does not appear to have an infectious or toxic origin, which narrows down the diﬀerential of eyelid edema. Thyroid eye disease (autoimmune) should always be high in the diﬀerential for noninfectious orbital inﬂammatory disease, and ﬂuctuating eyelid edema is a typical ocular sign for TED. While bilateral intermittent eyelid edema may be of allergic etiology, the history provided does not lead the examiner toward an allergic cause, and a patient with concurrent heart palpitations is more likely to have a diagnosis of thyroid disease. Therefore, thyroid function testing would be a better choice in the initial management of this patient's condition. It is important to remember that while this patient’s eyelid edema is described as symmetric, thyroid eye disease is frequently asymmetric. Furthermore, the severity of clinical ﬁndings does not parallel the patient’s serum thyroid studies. Finally, bilateral upper eyelid dermatochalasis necessitating blepharoplasty would not be an intermittent symptom, and thus blepharoplasty does not ﬁt for the management of this patient. If a thyroid patient does require surgery, the usual order is orbital decompression, followed by strabismus surgery, followed by eyelid surgery.
explanation: This patient presents with classic ﬁndings of involutional ptosis. As described, the levator muscle itself is normal, but the levator aponeurosis is stretched or disinserted, thus requiring advancement. Phenylephrine stimulates Müller muscle contraction and is a reasonable predictor of the eﬀect that a Müller muscle- conjunctival resection will have on the upper eyelid. Because phenylephrine did not elevate the eyelid eﬀectively in this patient, an external levator advancement is indicated. Frontalis sling is not indicated, because levator function is normal; frontalis slings are generally reserved for ptosis with poor levator function, which is classically congenital, traumatic, or neurogenic (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia [CPEO], myasthenia gravis). A brow lift would correct brow ptosis but not ptosis from levator dehiscence.

question: What vascular structure passes through the optic canal?
explanation: The ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal adjacent to the optic nerve. The recurrent branch of the middle meningeal artery, and the superior ophthalmic vein, pass through the superior ophthalmic ﬁssure. The inferior ophthalmic vein passes through the inferior ophthalmic ﬁssure.

question: The tram-track sign (parallel radiodense lines) on plain x-ray or computed tomography (CT) imaging suggests what orbital lesion?
explanation: The appearance of calciﬁcation of a meningioma on plain x-ray or CT is referred to as tram-tracking. Both CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans show diﬀuse tubular enlargement of the optic nerve with contrast enhancements, as well as parallel radiodense lines representing lesion edge calciﬁcation. Fibrous dysplasia characteristically has a ground- glass appearance on imaging with sparing of the soft tissues. Retinoblastoma usually shows calciﬁcations as well, but without the parallel radiodense lines. Cavernous hemangiomas are usually well encapsulated and intraconal.

question: A patient has eyelid malposition. The ophthalmologist recommends mucous membrane grafting with additional surgical repair. What eyelid malposition is most likely to lead to this recommendation?
explanation: In cases of cicatricial entropion, the shortened posterior lamella must be augmented to correct the lid malposition. This requires a mucous membrane graft. In contrast, cicatricial ectropion with anterior lamella deﬁciency requires a skin graft. Spastic entropion does not require tissue augmentation.

question: What is the primary cell type involved in lentigo maligna?
explanation: Lentigo maligna, also known as Hutchinson melanotic freckle or precancerous melanosis, is a ﬂat, irregularly shaped, unevenly pigmented, slowly enlarging lesion that typically occurs in the malar regions in older white persons. It is characterized by the radial, intraepidermal, uncontrolled growth phase of melanocytes. The absolute risk of lentigo maligna melanoma is approximately 2.0%-2.6%.

question: What acquired precancerous skin lesion can develop into a malignant melanoma?
explanation: Lentigo maligna is a ﬂat, irregularly shaped, unevenly pigmented, slowly enlarging lesion that typically occurs on the malar regions in older white persons. It diﬀers from senile or solar lentigo, in that lentigo maligna can present with signiﬁcant pigmentary variation, irregular borders, and progressive enlargement. The aﬀected area can extend beyond the visible area and can include the conjunctiva. Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion that may undergo degeneration to become a squamous cell carcinoma. These lesions typically are round, scaly plaques. Keratoacanthoma is regarded as a low-grade squamous cell carcinoma. These lesions typically appear as ﬂesh-colored papules that quickly evolve into nodules with keratin-ﬁlled craters and rolled borders.

question: Clinical evaluation of a 67- year-old woman reveals a slowly progressive left-sided proptosis of approximately 4 mm. She has full motility bilaterally. What imaging modality is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: CT is the most valuable technique overall for delineating the shape, location, extent, and character of lesions in the orbit. In addition to adequate soft tissue delineation, CT provides the most advanced assessment of bony anatomy of the available imaging modalities. CT helps reﬁne the diﬀerential diagnosis, and when orbitotomy is indicated, CT helps guide the selection of the surgical approach by showing the relationship of the lesion to the surgical space or spaces of the orbit. MRI provides better tissue contrast of structures in the orbital apex, intracanalicular portion of the optic nerve, structures in periorbital spaces, and orbitocranial tumors, as there is no artifact from the skull base bones. Further detail may be achieved with use of contrast, and it is not uncommon for both MRI and CT scans to be utilized in complete evaluation of an orbital disease process. However, as a ﬁrst step, CT yields greater value. Ultrasonography has high resolution in the area of the sclera and optic nerve insertion and is useful for evaluating scleritis and other anterior inﬂammation that produces ﬂuid in the sub-Tenon space. However, ultrasonography is of limited value in assessing lesions of the posterior orbit (because of sound attenuation) and is therefore not the ﬁrst step in evaluating an orbital process. Doppler ultrasonography is particularly useful for assessing orbital blood ﬂow, as might be desired in cases of carotid cavernous ﬁstulae or arteriovenous malformations. CT angiography or MR angiography can be used as a secondary diagnostic study in detection of arteriovenous malformations or ﬁstulas and aneurysms, but neither of them would be the most appropriate ﬁrst choice study.

explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor of childhood (average age at onset is 5–8 years). The typical presentation is a child with rapid-onset, progressive unilateral proptosis. Due to the extremely rapid growth of the tumor, these patients require immediate attention, with urgent imaging and biopsy. There is often reddish discoloration of the eyelids that is not accompanied by local heat or systemic fever, as it is in orbital cellulitis. Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma has a better prognosis (overall 5-year survival rate of about 90%) than does rhabdomyosarcoma occurring in other body sites. Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from primitive mesenchymal cells that diﬀerentiate toward skeletal muscle. There are 3 recognized histologic types of orbital rhabdomyosarcoma: embryonal (most common), alveolar (worst prognosis), and pleomorphic (best prognosis, least common). Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma may develop in the conjunctival stroma and may present as grapelike submucosal clusters (ie, botryoid variant). Histologically, spindle cells are arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations. These cross-striations are found in approximately 60% of embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas. Well- diﬀerentiated rhabdomyosarcomas feature numerous cells with well-deﬁned cross-striations. Immunohistochemically, rhabdomyosarcoma typically is positive for desmin, muscle- speciﬁc actin, vimentin, and myogenin. Before 1965, the standard treatment for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma was orbital exenteration, and the survival rate was poor. After 1965, radiation therapy and systemic chemotherapy became the mainstays of primary treatment, based on the guidelines set forth by the Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Study Group. Exenteration is reserved for recurrent cases.

Perineural spread of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) often presents in a subtle fashion, with complaints of tingling, numbness, and itching before progressing to pain.
